prompt: Which role decides which task runs on which executor?
hint: The master rents out cores and does not care what runs on them.

choices.text: Each worker, for the executors it started
choices.why: A worker starts executors and runs no tasks of its own.

choices.text: The driver
choices.why: Right. It holds the plan and sends each task to an executor itself.

choices.text: The executors, by taking turns among themselves
choices.why: Executors run what they are given; they do not plan.

choices.text: The master, which owns the cores
choices.why: The master assigns cores to applications and then stays out of the job.

prompt: Match each role to what it does.
hint: One plans, one rents, one offers, one works.

pairs.right: Plans the job and hands out its tasks
Hands out cores and memory to applications
Offers a machine's resources and starts processes on it
Runs one application's tasks, one per core

prompt: On YARN, what plays the part the standalone master plays in the lab?
hint: The words change between systems, the roles do not.

choices.text: Nothing; YARN has no central manager
choices.why: It has one, the ResourceManager, and lesson 12 runs it.

choices.text: The ResourceManager
choices.why: Yes. Its NodeManagers play the workers.

choices.text: The Spark driver, which YARN calls the master
choices.why: The driver keeps its name on every cluster manager.

choices.text: The NodeManager running on each machine
choices.why: That is YARN's worker, one per machine.

prompt: A job has 40 tasks of 3 seconds each on 4 cores. Ignoring overhead, how many seconds does it take?
hint: Count the waves first.

prompt: The same job with 41 tasks. Ignoring overhead, how many seconds now?
hint: One task more can mean one wave more.

prompt: A job has exactly as many tasks as cores, and one task's slice of data is twice as large as the others. What happens?
hint: Is there any other task to give the idle cores?

choices.text: Nothing changes, since the tasks run at the same time
choices.why: They start together, and the job ends when the last one does.

choices.text: The job takes twice as long, with idle cores waiting
choices.why: Right. With one wave there is nothing to rebalance onto the free cores.

choices.text: The scheduler splits it
choices.why: A task is the unit; the scheduler never splits one.

choices.text: The large task is killed and retried on a faster core
choices.why: Slow is not failed, and no core is faster for more data.

prompt: Why is splitting a job into a million tasks of a few milliseconds each a bad idea?
hint: What does each task cost besides its work?

choices.text: The fixed cost per task dominates
choices.why: Yes. Scheduling, starting and reporting are paid a million times.

choices.text: The answer becomes less precise
choices.why: The answer is the same; only the time changes.

choices.text: Spark refuses them
choices.why: It runs as many waves as needed.

choices.text: Each task needs its own executor and its own Java process
choices.why: An executor runs many tasks one after another.

prompt: Preferring an executor on the machine that holds a task's slice of data is called data ___.
hint: Where the data is.

prompt: While one job runs on the lab's cluster, how many Spark Java processes are on the machine?
hint: Master, workers, the driver and the executors.

prompt: What happens to the three executors when the job ends?
hint: Whose are they?

choices.text: They end with the application
choices.why: Right. Executors belong to one application; workers stay.

choices.text: They become workers
choices.why: Workers and executors are different processes with different jobs.

choices.text: They stay, ready for the next application
choices.why: The workers stay. Each application gets fresh executors.

choices.text: They are kept until the master is restarted
choices.why: The master does not hold executors at all.

prompt: The executors endpoint lists the driver with `totalCores` 0. Why?
hint: What does the driver do with the tasks?

choices.text: The REST endpoint cannot see the driver's cores
choices.why: It reports what Spark knows: the driver has no task slots.

choices.text: The driver had crashed
choices.why: The driver is the one answering the request.

choices.text: The driver runs no tasks; it hands them out
choices.why: Yes. Its work is planning and collecting.

choices.text: The driver gave its core to an executor when the job started
choices.why: Cores come from workers; the driver never had one to give.

prompt: A colleague's six-task job showed `WAITING` with zero cores. What caused it?
hint: How many cores did the first application take?

choices.text: Two applications cannot run on one cluster
choices.why: With a cap on the first, both ran at once.

choices.text: The first application took every core, as standalone allows by default
choices.why: Right. First come, first served, and the first came with no cap.

choices.text: The second job asked for more memory than a worker has
choices.why: It asked for the same 768 MB; the cores were the problem.

choices.text: The master was down
choices.why: The master answered and reported both applications.

prompt: With `spark.cores.max=2` on the large job, the small job finished in 14 s instead of 26. What did the large job pay?
hint: Count its waves on two cores.

choices.text: It failed halfway through and had to be resubmitted by hand the next morning
choices.why: It finished with the right answer.

choices.text: Nothing, because a cap only affects other applications
choices.why: The cap is on the large job itself; it ran on fewer cores.

choices.text: Its executors were given less memory each
choices.why: The cap is on cores; memory per executor stayed 768 MB.

choices.text: Fifteen waves instead of ten, and a longer run
choices.why: Yes. A cap is a decision about who waits.

prompt: Match each mechanism to what it shares.
hint: Some are between applications, one is inside one.

pairs.right: Caps one application's cores on standalone
A guaranteed share of the cluster per team
Jobs from different threads of one driver
Gives back executors an application is not using

prompt: If each machine fails once in 1,000 days on average, how many failures a day does a cluster of 5,000 machines see on average?
hint: Machines times the daily rate.

prompt: Put in order what a system for many machines does about a failure.
hint: You cannot redo what you have not identified.
items: Notice that a machine is gone
Know what was lost with it

prompt: Why can a job on 10,000 machines not simply be restarted from the beginning whenever any machine fails?
hint: How often would a four-hour run see a failure?

choices.text: Machines that fail are always slower to restart
choices.why: Restart speed is not the issue; the frequency is.

choices.text: At ten failures a day, a long run keeps meeting one
choices.why: Right. At ten failures a day, a four-hour run usually meets one.

choices.text: Restarting a job from the beginning is forbidden by the cluster manager
choices.why: Nothing forbids it; the arithmetic makes it hopeless.

choices.text: The data would be lost on restart
choices.why: The input is still there; the work done is what is lost.

prompt: A process killed by signal 9 is reported as exiting with code 128 + 9. What code is printed?
hint: Add.

prompt: A task sends one e-mail per row it processes. Its executor dies halfway and the task is retried. What is the risk?
hint: Spark assumes running a task twice is harmless.

choices.text: The job fails, since side effects are not allowed
choices.why: Spark does not detect side effects at all.

choices.text: None; a retry reuses the first attempt's results
choices.why: The first attempt's partial work died with the executor.

choices.text: Some people get the same e-mail twice
choices.why: Right. The retry repeats the side effect, and Spark cannot know.

choices.text: The retried task skips the rows already e-mailed
choices.why: Spark does not know which rows were e-mailed; it reruns the whole task.

prompt: Why does Spark give up after the same task fails four times?
hint: What does a task that fails everywhere suggest?

choices.text: The master forbids more than four executors per task
choices.why: The limit is the driver's setting, `spark.task.maxFailures`.

choices.text: The executors run out of memory after four attempts
choices.why: Attempts do not accumulate memory.

choices.text: Four is the number of workers in the lab
choices.why: The lab has three workers, and the default is four everywhere.

choices.text: It is likely a bug in the task, not a machine
choices.why: Yes. Retrying a bug only wastes the cluster.

prompt: After a worker died, the job still gave the right answer. Why was it slower?
hint: What replaced the lost worker?

choices.text: Nothing replaced it, so it ran on two cores
choices.why: Right. An executor can be restarted; a machine cannot be conjured.

choices.text: The master waited sixty seconds before noticing
choices.why: It noticed in seconds, because the connection closed.

choices.text: Every task was restarted from the very beginning
choices.why: Only the task on the lost executor ran again.

choices.text: The data had to be copied from the dead worker
choices.why: The input is on a disk every process shares here.

prompt: On a real cluster a machine loses power. Why does the master take longer to mark it dead than it did in the lab?
hint: What closed in the lab when the process was killed?

choices.text: It does not; a dead machine is noticed instantly everywhere
choices.why: Only when something tells the master; power loss tells nobody.

choices.text: Power loss is reported to the master by the operating system
choices.why: A machine without power reports nothing.

choices.text: The master checks workers only once a minute
choices.why: In the lab it noticed in seconds; the difference is the closed connection.

choices.text: No connection closes, so it waits for heartbeats to stop
choices.why: Yes. `spark.worker.timeout` is sixty seconds by default.

prompt: Why is a cluster sized so that the nightly jobs finish just in time a bad plan on a thousand machines?
hint: How often is every machine healthy?

choices.text: A thousand machines never fail at night
choices.why: Failures do not keep office hours.

choices.text: Jobs that finish early waste the money paid for machines left idle overnight
choices.why: The concern is lateness, not earliness.

choices.text: The master needs a spare machine of its own
choices.why: That is a separate concern about the master.

choices.text: Some machine is down on most nights, so jobs run late
choices.why: Right. Capacity has to include the machines that are broken.

prompt: After the driver was killed, the master listed the application as `FINISHED`. What does the lesson conclude?
hint: Who knows whether the job worked?

choices.text: The executors finished the job without the driver
choices.why: Executors exit when their driver vanishes.

choices.text: The master restarted the driver and the job completed
choices.why: Nothing restarted it; client mode has no supervision.

choices.text: The job finished before the kill reached it
choices.why: It printed no answer and its exit status was 137.

choices.text: Success is judged by the output and exit code, not the master
choices.why: Right. `FINISHED` only means no longer running.

prompt: In client mode, where does the driver run?
hint: Close the laptop and the job dies.

choices.text: On the master
choices.why: The master never runs drivers in client mode.

choices.text: Where `spark-submit` was typed
choices.why: Yes. In cluster mode the manager starts it on a worker instead.

choices.text: Inside the first executor that starts
choices.why: Executors run tasks, never the driver.

choices.text: On the worker with the most free memory
choices.why: That describes cluster mode, roughly.

prompt: What did the standalone master answer to `spark-submit --deploy-mode cluster tasks.py 3 1`?
hint: The language mattered.

choices.text: It refused: Python drivers are not supported that way
choices.why: Right. YARN and Kubernetes run Python drivers in cluster mode.

choices.text: It asked for ZooKeeper
choices.why: ZooKeeper is for standby masters, not for drivers.

choices.text: It ran the job in client mode instead, with a warning
choices.why: It stopped with an exception; nothing ran.

choices.text: It ran the driver on a worker and restarted it on failure
choices.why: That needs `--supervise` and a JVM program on standalone.

prompt: The lab's only master dies while a job is running. What happens to that job?
hint: Who does the driver talk to once it has executors?

choices.text: It dies at once, like a lost driver
choices.why: The master is out of the conversation once executors exist.

choices.text: It carries on, but lost executors cannot be replaced
choices.why: Right. The driver talks to its executors directly.

choices.text: It moves to a standby master automatically
choices.why: The lab has no standby; that needs ZooKeeper.

choices.text: It pauses every task until the master is back and every worker has registered again
choices.why: Tasks keep running on the executors it has.

prompt: Spark marked task 5 as speculatable but never launched a copy. Why?
hint: Where were all the executors?

choices.text: Speculation is off by default
choices.why: It was turned on with `spark.speculation=true`, and it marked the task.

choices.text: No core was free
choices.why: Two cores sat idle while task 5 slept.

choices.text: A copy never runs on the original's host, and all shared one
choices.why: Right. The commonest cause of a straggler is its machine.

choices.text: Task 5 was not slow enough to qualify
choices.why: It passed the threshold of about three seconds and was marked.

prompt: A task is slow because its slice holds the crawler's events. Does speculation help?
hint: What would the copy have to process?

choices.text: Yes; a copy on a healthy machine finishes sooner
choices.why: The machine was not the problem; the slice was.

choices.text: No, because speculation only works on Scala jobs
choices.why: It works for any job; the reason is the data.

choices.text: Yes, because the copy splits the slice in two
choices.why: A speculative copy is the same task on the same slice.

choices.text: No; the copy has the same data and is just as slow
choices.why: Right. Speculation cures sick machines, not heavy data. Lesson 8.

prompt: Match each event to what the job does about it.
hint: Which process holds the only copy of the plan?

pairs.right: Its tasks rerun and a new executor starts
Its tasks rerun on the cores that are left

pairs.left: One task is slow on a sick machine
pairs.right: A copy may run elsewhere, with speculation on

prompt: Order what happens when Ana runs `spark-submit tasks.py 60 1`, first to last.
hint: Resources before tasks.
items: The driver starts and asks the master for cores
Workers start executors for the application
The driver sends tasks to the executors
The executors exit with the application
